concept.name: Synthetic long stock
concept.definition: A synthetic long stock position is a long call and a short put at the same strike and expiration on the same underlying; by put-call parity its payoff replicates owning the underlying outright, gaining or losing point-for-point with the stock from the strike.
concept.intuition: You get the stock's payoff without buying the stock: above the strike you exercise into shares, below it the short put forces the purchase — either way you end up long at the strike.
concept.mechanics: At expiration the combined value equals S_T - K (plus any net premium adjustment), matching a forward purchase at K. The position requires no stock borrow and typically little capital upfront, but the short put carries full downside margin and assignment risk; unlike stock, the synthetic pays no dividends and confers no voting rights.
concept.formula: Value at expiration = max(S_T - K, 0) - max(K - S_T, 0) = S_T - K; initial cost C - P approximates S_0 - PV(K) by put-call parity.
concept.failure_modes: The short put leg is naked and margined, so a sharp decline generates losses and margin calls like leveraged stock ownership; early assignment on the ITM short put (e.g., deep ITM or rate-driven) collapses the synthetic into actual stock before expiration.
concept.misconceptions: A synthetic long is not free leverage: the position carries the full economic exposure of the stock minus dividends, and the apparent cheapness reflects deferred payment of the strike (financing), not a discount.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $100 call for $4.50 and sell the $100 put for $4.00 (net debit $0.50). If XYZ finishes at $110, the position is worth $10 for a $9.50 gain — matching 100 shares bought at $100 plus a small financing difference.
